Integer Rectangles: Two Proofs

InvariantsGraph TheoryLogic
Game: See why a rectangle tiled by rectangles with whole-number sides must itself have one.
How to play: Pick a tiling, switch on the graph or the special corners, and select a tile to change it.

Look for the math

Two short proofs of a surprising fact about tiling a rectangle with smaller rectangles.

The corner graph

Call a number special if it is a whole number (the argument works for any additive group). A tile whose width is special gets two horizontal edges joining its left and right corners; one whose height is special gets two vertical edges. An edge always joins two graph nodes that are both special. The big rectangle's four corners have degree 1, and every other node has degree 2 or 4, so a path starting at the lower-left corner can only get stuck at another corner of the big rectangle — which must therefore be special.

Counting corners

A special tile has 0, 2 or 4 special corners, so their total S is even. Counting the same corners as nodes gives S = S₁ + 2S₂ + 4S₄, where S₁ counts nodes seen once. Hence S₁ is even; since the lower-left corner is counted once, at least two big corners are special. The logic test checks both proofs on three tilings, including one where "special" means a multiple of one half.

Switch on the graph and follow the green path from the lower-left corner. Where does it stop?
